lead: A support is the part of a structure that touches the ground or another body. It stops some motions and lets others happen. In return, it pushes or pulls on the body with reaction forces, and sometimes with a reaction moment. The number of reactions is fixed by the support type, not by the load. Engineers use this count to draw a free body diagram correctly and to check whether a problem can be solved with statics alone. The same idea appears in a pole fixed to the ground, a bridge roller on a pier, and a door hinge.
prereq: You need: moment of a force about a point and the free body diagram from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Each support removes motion and gives reaction

blocks.text: A rigid body in a plane can slide along x, slide along y, and rotate. A support removes one or more of these motions. Each removed motion produces one reaction component. The reaction is the force or moment the support applies to the body.
In space a ball-and-socket support gives three force components. A fixed base gives three force components and three moment components. A smooth contact gives one force normal to the surface.
Follow these steps for every problem.

items: Isolate the body and sketch it alone.
Replace each support by the reaction components from the table.
Choose x and y axes and a positive sense for moments.
Assume a direction for each unknown and draw the arrow.
Write the equilibrium equations from Chapter 2.7.
Solve. If an answer is negative, keep the magnitude and reverse the arrow.

blocks.text: The assumed direction is free. Pick any arrow. A negative answer means the true direction is opposite. Keep the magnitude and reverse the arrow. Do not change the sign twice. Write the units on every reaction: N for force, N·m for moment. A reaction moment appears only where rotation is prevented.

The free body diagram is the bridge between the real structure and the equations. If the diagram is wrong, the algebra cannot save it. Check the count after drawing: one arrow for a roller, two for a pin, three for a fixed support.

For one rigid body in a plane, statics gives three equations: ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0, ΣM = 0. Count the unknown reaction components. Three unknowns: statics alone can solve the body. Fewer than three: the body is not fully restrained; it may be a mechanism. More than three: the body is statically indeterminate. You need extra information such as compatibility of deformation.

A pin plus a roller gives 2 + 1 = 3, determinate. A fixed support plus a roller gives 3 + 1 = 4, indeterminate to one degree. Two pins give 4, indeterminate unless an internal hinge supplies an extra equation.

Count before you solve. This habit saves time in exams and catches impossible models. A support that supplies more reactions than the body needs may still be safe, but the reactions depend on how the parts deform.
In space there are six equations. A ball-and-socket gives three unknowns. A fixed base gives six. Friction at a rough support is left to Unit 3.

figure.caption: A fixed base removes all three planar motions, a pin removes two translations, and a roller removes only the motion normal to the surface. The stack runs from most restraint at the top to least at the bottom.

spec.aria: A stack of supports from most to least restraint: fixed support with three reactions, pin with two, roller with one normal reaction.

examples.question: A vertical pole AB is 3 m tall. It is fixed to the ground at A. At the free top end B, a horizontal force of 200 N acts to the right and a vertical load of 500 N acts downward. Find the reaction force and reaction moment at A.
steps: Draw the pole alone. At A the fixed support can give A<sub>x</sub>, A<sub>y</sub> and M<sub>A</sub>. Assume A<sub>x</sub> to the right, A<sub>y</sub> upward, and M<sub>A</sub> anticlockwise.
ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0: A<sub>x</sub> + 200 N = 0, so A<sub>x</sub> = −200 N. The minus sign means 200 N to the left.
ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0: A<sub>y</sub> − 500 N = 0, so A<sub>y</sub> = 500 N upward.
Take moments about A. The 200 N force acts at height 3 m. Its moment is 3 m × 200 N = 600 N·m clockwise.
The 500 N load acts along the pole. Its line of action passes through A, so its moment about A is zero.
ΣM<sub>A</sub> = 0: M<sub>A</sub> − 600 N·m = 0, so M<sub>A</sub> = 600 N·m anticlockwise.
examples.answer: At A: 200 N to the left, 500 N upward, and a 600 N·m anticlockwise moment.
examples.check:
Fx = 200
Fy = 500
h = 3
Ax_mag = abs(Fx)
Ay = Fy
M_A = h * Fx
print(Ax_mag)
print(Ay)
print(M_A)

traps: A pin or hinge gets two force components, never a moment. If you add M at a pin, you have changed it into a fixed support.
A roller on a horizontal floor gives one vertical force. On an inclined surface the force is perpendicular to the surface, not vertical. It has both x and y components.
A negative reaction is not an error. It means the true direction is opposite to your arrow. Keep the magnitude and reverse the arrow.

More than three unknown reactions on one planar body does not always mean the problem is impossible; it means statics alone is not enough. Check for extra equations from another body or an internal hinge before calling it indeterminate.
Moment is in N·m and force is in N. Do not add them, and do not drop the units in the final answer.

quiz.q: How many reaction components does a smooth roller support give in a plane problem?
quiz.a: One reaction component: a force normal to the surface.

quiz.q: Why does a fixed support give a moment reaction while a pin does not?
quiz.a: A fixed support prevents rotation as well as both translations. A pin allows rotation, so it gives only two force components.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam has a pin at A and a roller at B on a horizontal surface. How many unknown reaction components are at A and B together? Is the beam statically determinate?
quiz.a: Pin A gives A<sub>x</sub> and A<sub>y</sub> (2). Roller B gives B<sub>y</sub> (1). Total 3. A planar rigid body has 3 equations, so yes, it is determinate.

quiz.q: An inclined surface makes 30° with the horizontal. A roller rests on it. The roller reaction has magnitude 400 N. Find its horizontal and vertical components.
quiz.a: The reaction is perpendicular to the surface, so it makes 30° with the vertical. Horizontal = 400 sin 30° = 200 N. Vertical = 400 cos 30° = 346.4 N.

quiz.q: A body has a fixed support and a roller. It carries no other unknown. Can statics alone find all reactions? Explain with a count.
quiz.a: Fixed gives 3 unknowns. Roller gives 1. Total 4. A single planar rigid body has 3 equilibrium equations. The body is statically indeterminate to one degree; statics alone cannot find all four.

quiz.q: A rigid bar AB is supported by a pin at A and a pin at B. A load acts at midspan. Is the problem statically determinate? What changes if B is a roller on a horizontal surface?
quiz.a: Two pins give 4 unknowns, so the bar alone is indeterminate. Replace B by a roller: B<sub>x</sub> disappears, leaving A<sub>x</sub>, A<sub>y</sub>, B<sub>y</sub>, 3 unknowns. The bar becomes determinate.

quiz.q: A student assumes A<sub>x</sub> to the right and gets A<sub>x</sub> = −150 N. What does the answer mean?
quiz.a: The reaction is 150 N to the left. The negative sign reverses the assumed direction.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real supports are never perfectly ideal. A bridge bearing allows thermal expansion, but it also has friction and may lock after years of dirt and corrosion. Buildings settle, so a fixed base may rotate a little. Computer models of frames and machines replace each support by constraint equations, and the same count of unknowns decides whether the solver needs extra compatibility conditions. Search next for support reactions, statically indeterminate structures and finite element boundary conditions.
